entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go beyond what is acceptable, polite or allowed, especially in behavior or remarks.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, workplace complaints and news about jokes, criticism or behavior: *That comment crossed the line.* Both *cross the line* and *cross a line* are used, often with *into*: *crossed the line into harassment*. It is a firm judgment, so saying it to someone directly signals that you are really offended.
entries.pattern: cross the line / a line (into + something worse)
examples: Teasing is fine, but making fun of his stutter **crossed the line**.
The coach **crossed the line** when he started screaming at a twelve-year-old.
Critics say the tabloid **crossed the line** from reporting into harassment.

drill.sentence: I don't mind my sister borrowing my clothes, but reading my diary {{crossed the line}}.
drill.hint: went beyond what is acceptable (not *went too far*)

entries.related: *go too far* — very similar; *overstep your bounds* — act beyond your authority; *draw a line in the sand* — set a limit that others must not cross.

entries.term: draw a line in the sand
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To set a firm limit or condition and make clear that you will not accept anything beyond it.
entries.usage: Common in politics, negotiations, parenting and relationships. It sounds firm, sometimes confrontational, and implies consequences if the limit is crossed. The related noun *a red line* is common in diplomacy.
examples: After years of late-night calls, Maria finally **drew a line in the sand**: no work email after seven p.m.
The union **drew a line in the sand** over health benefits and refused any cuts.
The publisher **drew a line in the sand** and refused to extend the deadline again.

drill.sentence: My sister let her kids stay up later and later until she finally {{drew a line in the sand}} at nine o'clock.
drill.hint: set a firm limit (not *put her foot down*)

entries.related: *a red line* — a limit, used especially in diplomacy; *put your foot down* — firmly refuse to allow something; *cross the line* — go beyond what is acceptable.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act very carefully between two opposite risks, extremes or demands, so as not to go too far in either direction.
entries.usage: Common in news, politics, parenting and work. The usual pattern is *walk a fine line between A and B*: *She walks a fine line between honesty and tact.* *Tread a fine line* is a more British variant.
entries.pattern: walk a fine line between A and B
examples: Parents of teenagers **walk a fine line** between giving them freedom and keeping them safe.
The central bank is **walking a fine line**, trying to fight inflation without causing a recession.
Good comedians **walk a fine line** between edgy and offensive.

drill.sentence: As a referee, you {{walk a fine line}} between controlling the game and letting the players play.
drill.hint: have to balance carefully between two extremes (not *… a tightrope*)

entries.related: *walk a tightrope* — be in a risky position where balance is needed; *tread a fine line* — same, more British; *strike a balance* — find a good compromise between two things.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do the hardest, most demanding or most important part of a job or task.
entries.usage: Common in American work, politics and sports talk, often with *most of*, *all of* or *the real*: *She did most of the heavy lifting.* It is usually figurative, not about carrying things. Tools and systems can be the subject too: *the software does the heavy lifting*.
entries.pattern: do (most of / all of) the heavy lifting (on something)
examples: My wife **did the heavy lifting** on our tax return; I just signed it.
Our defense **did the heavy lifting** tonight, so we only needed one goal to win.
In this app, the cloud **does the heavy lifting**, so it runs fine on old phones.

drill.sentence: Grandpa came up with the idea for the reunion, but Aunt Rosa {{did the heavy lifting}}: booking the hall, the food and the hotel rooms.
drill.hint: handled the hardest parts of the job (not *did the legwork*)

entries.related: *carry the load* — do most of the work; *do the legwork* — do the practical, often boring work of gathering information; *pull your weight* — do your fair share.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A situation in which two things depend on each other, so it is impossible to say which causes the other or which must come first.
entries.usage: Common in business, medicine and everyday reasoning when cause and effect run both ways. It also appears as *a chicken-and-egg situation* or *question*. Do not confuse it with *a catch-22*, which is a trap created by contradictory rules.
examples: My band had **a chicken-and-egg problem**: clubs wouldn't book us without fans, and we couldn't get fans without gigs.
Doctors see **a chicken-and-egg problem** with poor sleep and anxiety, since each one makes the other worse.
Electric cars and charging stations were **a chicken-and-egg problem** for years: few drivers meant few chargers, and few chargers meant few drivers.

drill.sentence: Do kids read less because they don't enjoy it, or do they not enjoy it because they read so little? It's {{a chicken-and-egg problem}}.
drill.hint: unclear which one causes the other (not *a vicious circle*)

entries.related: *a vicious circle* — two problems that keep making each other worse; *a catch-22* — a trap created by contradictory rules; *cause and effect* — the plain, neutral term.
entries.origin: From the old riddle *Which came first, the chicken or the egg?*

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Said to ask people not to blame you or get angry with you for bad news that you are only passing on.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, usually said by the person delivering the news, as a light, half-joking defense. It also works as a criticism: *shooting the messenger* means punishing the person who reported a problem instead of fixing the problem.
examples: **Don't shoot the messenger**, but the restaurant just called to say they lost our reservation.
Hey, **don't shoot the messenger**; I'm just telling you what the mechanic said.
Instead of fixing the safety problems, the company fired the whistleblower — a classic case of **shooting the messenger**.

drill.sentence: {{Don't shoot the messenger}}, but Mom says we have to spend the whole weekend at Aunt Linda's.
drill.hint: please, no anger at me for bringing the news (not *blame me*)

entries.related: *don't blame me* — plainer; *break the news* — tell someone bad news; *take the heat* — accept criticism, often for others.
entries.origin: The idea is ancient: Sophocles and Plutarch both describe messengers who were blamed or punished for bringing bad news.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To stop doing something that is failing, so that you do not lose even more money, time or effort.
entries.usage: Common in business, investing, relationships and everyday decisions: *It's time to cut our losses.* It presents accepting a loss now as the smarter choice and often follows *decide to*, *time to* or *just*. The possessive matches the subject: *they cut their losses*.
examples: The stock kept falling, so I **cut my losses** and sold at twenty dollars a share.
After the third bad date, she decided to **cut her losses** and stop seeing him.
The company **cut its losses** and closed its stores in Europe after three bad years.

drill.sentence: We'd already waited two hours in line for the ride, but with the park closing soon, we decided to {{cut our losses}} and leave.
drill.hint: stop before wasting even more time (not *call it a day* or *call it quits*)

entries.related: *throw good money after bad* — keep spending on something that is failing; *call it quits* — stop doing something; *the sunk cost fallacy* — continuing because of what you have already spent.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Deciding whether something will succeed or fail completely, with no middle result.
entries.usage: Common in sports, business and journalism, mostly before a noun with hyphens: *a make-or-break game*, *a make-or-break moment*. After *be*, the hyphens are usually dropped: *This season is make or break for the coach.* It adds drama and urgency.
entries.pattern: a make-or-break + moment / year / deal; be make or break for someone
examples: Sunday's game is **make or break**: win and we're in the playoffs; lose and the season's over.
For many small retailers, the holiday shopping season is **make-or-break** time.
Moving in together was a **make-or-break** moment for our relationship.

drill.sentence: Reviews from the first few weeks are often {{make or break}} for a new restaurant.
drill.hint: decide total success or total failure (not *crucial* or *decisive*)

entries.related: *do or die* — a situation where you must succeed or face disaster; *a turning point* — a moment when things change; *all or nothing* — complete success or complete failure, with no middle.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To avoid being noticed by people in authority, the media or the public, sometimes on purpose.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, business and sports journalism. It can be positive (a hidden gem, a modest person) or suggest that someone is avoiding control or rules. *Stay under the radar* and *slip under the radar* are common variants.
examples: This little taco place has **flown under the radar** for years, but now there's a line every night.
He's one of the best players in the league, but he **flies under the radar** because he plays in a small market.
For months, the scam **flew under the radar** of state regulators.

drill.sentence: Keep the party off social media. If it {{flies under the radar}}, my parents will never find out.
drill.hint: avoids attention (not *stays …* or *goes unnoticed*)

entries.related: *keep a low profile* — deliberately avoid attention; *go unnoticed* — plainer; *on someone's radar* — the opposite, noticed or considered by someone.
entries.origin: From military aircraft flying low to avoid being detected by enemy radar.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The overall situation and its most important aspects, rather than the small details.
entries.usage: Very common at work, in politics and in personal advice: *Let's look at the big picture.* Typical verbs are *see*, *look at*, *focus on* and *lose sight of*. With a hyphen it works as an adjective: *a big-picture thinker*.
examples: Don't stress about one bad grade. Look at **the big picture**: you're doing really well.
Our CEO is great at **the big picture** but terrible with details.
Fighting about the guest list made us lose sight of **the big picture**: we're getting married!

drill.sentence: One rainy day doesn't ruin a two-week vacation; try to focus on {{the big picture}} instead of the weather.
drill.hint: the overall situation, not the details

entries.related: *can't see the forest for the trees* — be too focused on details to understand the whole; *in the grand scheme of things* — when everything is considered; *the nitty-gritty* — the practical details.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The minimum features or conditions you need just to take part or compete, which give you no special advantage.
entries.usage: Business and tech jargon, common in American meetings and product talk: *Mobile ordering is table stakes for restaurants now.* It usually follows *be*, often with *just* or *now*, and stresses that something once special is now expected. Outside business it can sound like corporate jargon.
examples: Free Wi-Fi used to impress hotel guests; now it's **table stakes**.
Good security is **table stakes** for any cloud product; it won't win you customers by itself.
In this city, good credit is just **table stakes** for renting; landlords also want three months' rent up front.

drill.sentence: For a youth soccer coach, being on time and organized is just {{table stakes}}; the real test is keeping twenty kids motivated.
drill.hint: the basic minimum needed to take part — business jargon (not *the bare minimum* or *a given*)

entries.related: *a given* — something everyone assumes; *the bare minimum* — the least you can do; *a differentiator* — business jargon, a feature that sets you apart.

entries.term: get to the bottom of something
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To find out the real cause of a problem or the full truth about a situation.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and customer service, often as a promise: *We'll get to the bottom of this.* It suggests a careful investigation, with *this*, *it* or *what happened* as the usual object. It sounds determined and sometimes a little dramatic.
entries.pattern: get to the bottom of + this / it / what happened
examples: The plumber spent all morning trying to **get to the bottom of** the leak in our ceiling.
Police say they're determined to **get to the bottom of** the warehouse fire.
Someone ate my lunch from the office fridge, and I'm going to **get to the bottom of** it.

drill.sentence: The vet ran a few blood tests to {{get to the bottom of}} why our cat had stopped eating.
drill.hint: discover the real cause of (not *figure out*)

entries.related: *figure out* — understand or solve, plainer; *get to the root of* — find the basic cause of a problem; *dig deeper* — investigate more carefully.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A no-win situation in which you cannot do one thing until you have done another, but the second depends on the first.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism about rules, bureaucracy and jobs: *It's a catch-22.* It often follows *a classic* or *a real*, and the capitalized *Catch-22* is also correct. Use it for a trap created by contradictory rules or conditions, not for any hard choice.
examples: It's **a catch-22**: you can't get a job without experience, and you can't get experience without a job.
To open a bank account, I needed a local address, but every landlord wanted a bank account first — **a real catch-22**.
Patients face **a catch-22**: insurance won't pay for the new drug until cheaper ones fail, but those may be unsafe for them.

drill.sentence: My doctor won't refill the prescription without an appointment, and the next opening is after I run out. It's {{a catch-22}}.
drill.hint: a trap created by contradictory conditions — a novel title (not *a no-win situation*)

entries.related: *a no-win situation* — plainer; *a chicken-and-egg problem* — unclear which of two things comes first; *a double bind* — a situation where every choice is bad.
entries.origin: From Joseph Heller's 1961 novel *Catch-22*, in which a pilot who asks to stop flying combat missions is considered sane and therefore must keep flying.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To reach a crisis point at which a problem that has been growing can no longer be ignored and action must be taken.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and family stories: *Tensions came to a head at Thursday's meeting.* The subject is usually a problem, conflict or tension, often with *finally*. *Bring something to a head* means to cause that crisis.
examples: Years of noise complaints **came to a head** when the neighbors called the police on the band.
Tensions between the owner and the head coach **came to a head** after the playoff loss.
The fight over who would care for Mom finally **came to a head** at Thanksgiving.

drill.sentence: The dispute between the city and the garbage collectors {{came to a head}} last week, when trash piled up on every corner.
drill.hint: reached a crisis point (not *boiled over*)

entries.related: *boil over* — suddenly turn into anger or violence; *reach a breaking point* — become impossible to bear; *bring something to a head* — force a crisis.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deal with urgent problems one after another as they come up, with no time for planning or bigger goals.
entries.usage: Common in American workplace talk, often as a complaint: *I spent all day putting out fires.* It suggests reacting instead of planning, so it describes a stressful, unproductive day. The noun *firefighting* is used in the same sense.
entries.pattern: spend the day / be busy putting out fires
examples: I meant to work on the budget, but I spent the whole day **putting out fires**.
With three kids under six, most of our evenings are just **putting out fires**.
The new principal has been **putting out fires** since day one, from a broken boiler to a bus strike.

drill.sentence: I'd love to plan the move properly, but right now I'm too busy {{putting out fires}} with the movers, the bank and the kids' new school.
drill.hint: handling one urgent problem after another — an emergency-crew image

entries.related: *firefighting* — the noun, in the same sense; *damage control* — trying to limit harm after something goes wrong; *juggle* — handle several tasks at once.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To shift responsibility or blame for something to someone else, instead of dealing with it yourself.
entries.usage: Critical, common in politics, bureaucracy and workplace complaints: *Stop passing the buck.* It often takes *to* + the other person or department. The famous opposite is President Truman's desk sign, *The buck stops here*.
examples: When I called about the bill, the phone company kept **passing the buck** from one department to another.
When our bags went missing, the airline **passed the buck** to the airport.
Parents and schools often **pass the buck** to each other when a kid is struggling.

drill.sentence: Every time the elevator breaks, the building manager and the repair company {{pass the buck}}, and nothing gets fixed.
drill.hint: shift responsibility to the other side (not *point fingers*)

entries.related: *point the finger at* — blame someone; *the buck stops here* — I accept final responsibility; *shirk responsibility* — formal, avoid a duty.
entries.origin: From poker, where a marker called the *buck* showed whose turn it was to deal and was passed to the next player.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To do the work that someone else is not doing or cannot do, so that the job still gets done.
entries.usage: Common at work, at home and in sports, often with a hint of complaint: *I'm tired of picking up the slack for him.* The pattern is *pick up the slack (for someone)*. *Take up the slack* is a less common variant.
examples: When my sister moved away, I had to **pick up the slack** in caring for our parents.
With two nurses out sick, the rest of the staff **picked up the slack**.
Our best player is injured, so the younger guys will need to **pick up the slack**.

drill.sentence: My roommate never cleans the kitchen, so I'm always {{picking up the slack}} for her.
drill.hint: doing the work she doesn't do (not *covering*)

entries.related: *cover for someone* — do someone's work while they are away; *carry the load* — do most of the work; *pull your weight* — do your fair share.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To annoy or irritate someone strongly, often in a way they find hard to ignore.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about people and habits that bother you, often with *really*: *his attitude really gets under my skin*. It also describes deliberate provoking: *Don't let him get under your skin*. In a different, positive sense it can mean that someone or something affects you deeply, but the annoyed sense is more common.
examples: It really **gets under my skin** when people talk during movies.
Don't let the other team's trash talk **get under your skin**.
The heckler's mocking tone clearly **got under the comedian's skin**.

drill.sentence: Her habit of answering every question with another question really {{gets under my skin}}.
drill.hint: annoys me deeply (not *… on my nerves*)

entries.related: *get on someone's nerves* — annoy someone, often through repetition; *push someone's buttons* — annoy someone on purpose; *rub someone the wrong way* — irritate someone, often without meaning to.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To deliberately say or do things that you know will make someone angry or upset.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about family, partners and coworkers, often with *know how to*: *She knows exactly how to push my buttons.* It stresses that the person knows your weak spots and uses them on purpose. *Know which buttons to push* is a common variant.
examples: My mom knows how to **push my buttons** — one comment about my hair and I'm furious.
The talk show host loves to **push his guests' buttons** to get a dramatic reaction.
Toddlers test limits and **push your buttons**; it's part of growing up.

drill.sentence: Ignore him when he makes jokes about your job. He's just trying to {{push your buttons}}.
drill.hint: make you angry on purpose (not *get a rise out of you*)

entries.related: *get a rise out of someone* — provoke an angry reaction on purpose; *get under someone's skin* — annoy someone, not always on purpose; *hit a nerve* — upset someone by touching a sensitive topic.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To upset someone or cause a strong reaction by mentioning a subject that is sensitive for them.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and journalism, and often unintentional: *My question about his divorce hit a nerve.* *Touch a nerve* and *strike a nerve* are common variants. It can also describe a story or comment that gets a strong public reaction: *The article hit a nerve with readers.*
examples: When I asked about his old job, I could tell I'd **hit a nerve**.
The documentary about student debt **hit a nerve** with millions of young viewers.
Mentioning her weight at the family dinner really **hit a nerve**.

drill.sentence: My joke about his bald spot clearly {{hit a nerve}}; he didn't speak to me for the rest of the evening.
drill.hint: upset him by mentioning a sensitive topic (not *struck …* or *touched …*)

entries.related: *touch a nerve* / *strike a nerve* — same meaning; *a sore spot* — a topic that upsets someone; *push someone's buttons* — upset someone on purpose.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Something that keeps changing, so it is hard to deal with, measure or aim for.
entries.usage: Common at work, in policy and in planning, often with mild frustration about constant change: *The requirements are a moving target.* It usually follows *be* or appears in *like trying to hit a moving target*. It can describe goals, prices, rules, deadlines or people's expectations.
examples: With prices rising every month, our grocery budget is **a moving target**.
The client's requirements were **a moving target**, so the project ran months over schedule.
Keeping up with my teenager's slang is like trying to hit **a moving target**.

drill.sentence: Every time I've almost saved enough for a down payment, home prices jump again. It's {{a moving target}}.
drill.hint: something that keeps changing, so you can't reach it (not *a losing battle*)

entries.related: *move the goalposts* — change the rules or the target on purpose; *in flux* — constantly changing, more formal; *a losing battle* — a fight you cannot win.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To say that you support an idea or cause without actually doing anything to help it or follow it.
entries.usage: Critical, used in politics, business and journalism about promises that are not backed by action. The pattern is *pay lip service to* + noun, often with *only* or *just*. It is formal enough for writing and sounds cynical.
entries.pattern: pay (only) lip service to + idea / cause / value
examples: The company **pays lip service to** work-life balance but still emails people at midnight.
City hall **pays lip service to** fixing the roads, but the potholes are still everywhere.
He **pays lip service to** eating healthy, then orders fries with everything.

drill.sentence: The league says it cares about player safety, but critics say it only {{pays lip service to}} the issue.
drill.hint: expresses support for … without any real action

entries.related: *talk the talk* — say the right things, often in *talk the talk but not walk the walk*; *empty promises* — promises that won't be kept; *window dressing* — something done only to look good.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A fresh start in which past mistakes, debts or problems are forgotten or no longer count.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and law. Typical patterns are *start with a clean slate*, *get a clean slate* and *wipe the slate clean*. It is positive and is often used about new jobs, relationships, school years or criminal records.
examples: Moving to a new city felt like **a clean slate** after my divorce.
The bank agreed to waive the late fees and give us **a clean slate**.
Our new manager said we'd all start with **a clean slate**, whatever happened under the old boss.

drill.sentence: Let's forget about last year's argument and start over with {{a clean slate}}.
drill.hint: a new beginning with the past forgotten (not *a fresh start*)

entries.related: *a fresh start* — plainer; *wipe the slate clean* — forgive or forget past mistakes; *turn over a new leaf* — start behaving better.
entries.origin: From the slate boards once used in schools and taverns for writing, which could be wiped clean.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To begin to improve or recover after a difficult period, such as an illness or a crisis.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and talk about health: *the economy has finally turned the corner*. It often comes with *finally*, or in a cautious question: *Have we turned the corner yet?* It suggests that the worst is over, so it sounds hopeful but careful.
examples: After two weeks in the hospital, Dad has finally **turned the corner**.
Economists say the housing market may have **turned the corner**.
The team looked hopeless in October, but they've **turned the corner** with five straight wins.

drill.sentence: Our little bakery lost money for two years, but this spring we {{turned the corner}} and started making a profit.
drill.hint: began to improve after a hard time (with *the*)

entries.related: *bounce back* — recover quickly; *the worst is over* — plainer; *see the light at the end of the tunnel* — see signs that a hard period is ending.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To gradually gain speed, energy, popularity or support.
entries.usage: Common in news, business and sports, often in the progressive, with movements, campaigns, economies or projects as subjects: *The campaign is picking up steam.* *Gather steam* and *pick up speed* are similar. *Run out of steam* is the opposite.
examples: The campaign to save the old theater is **picking up steam**; we already have five thousand signatures.
Home sales started **picking up steam** again after interest rates fell.
The party was slow at first, but it **picked up steam** once the band arrived.

drill.sentence: Pickleball had been growing slowly for years, then it suddenly {{picked up steam}} and courts started appearing in every park.
drill.hint: grew faster and stronger — a train image (not *took off*)

entries.related: *gain momentum* — more formal; *gather steam* — same; *run out of steam* — the opposite, lose energy.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A guess made with little or no information, so it is unlikely to be right.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often to admit you're guessing: *This is a shot in the dark, but …* It can also describe an attempt with little chance of success, such as applying for a job you probably won't get. It sounds modest and friendly, so it softens questions and requests.
examples: This is **a shot in the dark**, but did anyone find a black umbrella in the lobby?
Sending my résumé to the famous chef was **a shot in the dark**, but she called me back.
My answer to the last trivia question was **a total shot in the dark**, and it was right.

drill.sentence: I had no idea which country the painter was from, so I just took {{a shot in the dark}} and said Portugal.
drill.hint: a guess with almost no information (not *a wild guess* or *a stab*)

entries.related: *a wild guess* — plainer; *take a stab at* — try or guess without much confidence; *a long shot* — something with little chance of success.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To narrowly avoid a bad situation or a serious problem, often without realizing the danger until later.
entries.usage: Very common in American conversation, usually looking back: *I really dodged a bullet there.* It is used for jobs you didn't get, partners you didn't marry, storms that missed and similar escapes. Don't mix it up with *bite the bullet*, which means forcing yourself to do something unpleasant.
examples: I almost bought a condo in that building; after the flood, I realized I'd **dodged a bullet**.
The hurricane turned east at the last minute, and the city **dodged a bullet**.
I didn't get the job, and six months later the company went bankrupt. I **dodged a bullet**.

drill.sentence: The restaurant we almost booked for our anniversary got shut down for health violations. We really {{dodged a bullet}}.
drill.hint: narrowly avoided something bad (not *got lucky*)

entries.related: *a close call* — a situation where something bad almost happened; *a narrow escape* — similar, more neutral; *bite the bullet* — a different idiom: force yourself to do something unpleasant.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To start going badly wrong, or, about a person, to start behaving in a wild or out-of-control way.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news about plans, meetings, campaigns and people's lives: *The meeting went off the rails after ten minutes.* About a person, it suggests losing control, often with drinking, drugs or anger. It is stronger than *off track*, which just means not progressing as planned.
examples: The dinner party **went off the rails** when my uncle started talking about politics.
After his divorce, he **went off the rails** for a while: late nights, heavy drinking, missed work.
The peace talks **went off the rails** when one side walked out.

drill.sentence: Our road trip {{went off the rails}} on day two, when the car broke down in a snowstorm.
drill.hint: started going badly wrong — a train image (not *… south*)

entries.related: *go south* — go wrong, often gradually; *spiral out of control* — get worse very quickly; *derail* — make something go off course.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To go wrong, get worse or lose value.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and business talk about deals, relationships, markets and plans: *Things went south after the merger.* It is casual and usually in the past tense, with subjects like *things*, *the deal* or *the economy*. *Head south* is a variant, especially for prices and numbers.
examples: The date started well, but things **went south** when he started talking about his ex.
Their business partnership **went south** after a fight over money.
My grades **went south** after I started working thirty hours a week.

drill.sentence: The barbecue was going great until it started pouring and the grill caught fire; then everything {{went south}}.
drill.hint: got much worse — a direction on a map (not *downhill*)

entries.related: *go downhill* — get gradually worse; *go off the rails* — go badly wrong, often out of control; *take a turn for the worse* — suddenly become worse, often about health.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Until the very last moment, with the result still uncertain.
entries.usage: Common in sports, elections, negotiations and deadlines, usually after *go* or *come*: *The race went down to the wire.* Before a noun it takes hyphens: *a down-to-the-wire finish*. It suggests tension and uncertainty, not just lateness.
entries.pattern: go / come down to the wire
examples: The championship game **went down to the wire**, with the winning goal in the final seconds.
Budget negotiations in Congress are once again coming **down to the wire**.
Packing for the move came **down to the wire**: we taped the last box as the truck pulled up.

drill.sentence: Our fantasy football league went {{down to the wire}} and was decided by the very last game of the season.
drill.hint: to the very last moment, still undecided — a horse-racing image

entries.related: *neck and neck* — exactly even in a race; *too close to call* — so even that nobody can predict the winner; *at the eleventh hour* — at the last possible moment.
entries.origin: From horse racing, where a wire stretched above the finish line marked the end of the race.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To prepare for every possible situation or problem, so that nothing goes wrong unexpectedly.
entries.usage: Common in American work, travel and planning talk: *We want to cover all our bases before the inspection.* *Cover all the bases* is just as common, and *cover your bases* is shorter. It sounds careful and practical, sometimes a little defensive.
examples: We booked a refundable hotel and bought travel insurance to **cover all our bases**.
The lawyer asked a hundred questions just to **cover all her bases** before the trial.
I made a vegetarian dish and a gluten-free one to **cover all the bases** at the potluck.

drill.sentence: Before the interview, she researched the company, practiced her answers and printed extra copies of her résumé, just to {{cover all her bases}}.
drill.hint: prepare for every possibility — a baseball image (not *be on the safe side*)

entries.related: *be on the safe side* — take precautions just in case; *leave no stone unturned* — try every possible way; *have a plan B* — have a backup plan.
entries.origin: From baseball, where fielders must be ready to protect every base.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Wrong or mistaken, especially in a guess, judgment or accusation.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and debate, often with *way*, *completely* or *a little*: *You're way off base.* It usually follows *be* and describes people, comments, guesses or claims. It can sound blunt, so *I think you're a bit off base* is a softer form.
examples: If you think I'm angry about the money, you're **way off base**.
The critics were **off base**; the movie turned out to be a huge hit.
The rumor that the bakery is closing is completely **off base**; they're just remodeling.

drill.sentence: My dad assumed my new friend was a bad influence, but he was completely {{off base}}: she got me to study more.
drill.hint: mistaken — a baseball image (not *off the mark*)

entries.related: *off the mark* — inaccurate; *wide of the mark* — far from correct, more British; *on the money* — the opposite, exactly right.
entries.origin: From baseball, where a runner caught off base can be tagged out.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: An impressive achievement that needed a lot of skill, effort or courage.
entries.usage: Common in praise, news and speeches: *Running a marathon at seventy is no small feat.* It follows *be* and often comes after a comma with *which is*: *…, which is no small feat*. The British equivalent is *no mean feat*.
examples: Raising four kids on one income is **no small feat**.
She finished medical school while working nights, which is **no small feat**.
Getting a table at that restaurant on a Friday night is **no small feat**.

drill.sentence: Climbing Mount Rainier at sixty-eight is {{no small feat}}, and my grandfather did it twice.
drill.hint: an impressive achievement — the American form (not *no easy task*)

entries.related: *no mean feat* — the British form; *quite an accomplishment* — plainer; *a tall order* — a hard task before it is done.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The people or organizations in authority who make the important decisions, often seen as distant or impersonal.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and at work, usually ironic or mildly critical, for bosses, officials or institutions you can't influence: *The powers that be decided to close the cafeteria.* It always takes *the* and a plural verb. It lets you complain without naming a specific person.
examples: **The powers that be** have decided we all need to be back in the office four days a week.
I'd love to keep the library open on Sundays, but that's up to **the powers that be** at city hall.
Some fans think **the powers that be** in the league want the big-market teams to win.

drill.sentence: Our flight was canceled, and the gate agent said the decision came from {{the powers that be}} at headquarters.
drill.hint: the people in authority (not *the higher-ups*)

entries.related: *the higher-ups* — informal, senior people in an organization; *the establishment* — the powerful groups in a society; *the brass* — informal, top officers or managers.
entries.origin: From the King James Bible (Romans 13:1): *the powers that be are ordained of God*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To take a risk and hope that things will turn out well, even though the result is uncertain.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, sports and business: *We decided to roll the dice and move to Austin.* It often takes *on* + the risky option: *roll the dice on a young quarterback*. It sounds bold or slightly reckless.
examples: We **rolled the dice** on a cheap rental in Rome, and it turned out to be great.
The team **rolled the dice** on an unknown quarterback in the draft.
Quitting my job to start a landscaping business meant **rolling the dice** with our savings.

drill.sentence: Nobody knew if the new menu would work, but the owner decided to {{roll the dice}} anyway.
drill.hint: take a risk and hope for the best — a board-game image (not *take a gamble*)

entries.related: *take a gamble* — take a risk; *take the plunge* — finally do something big and risky; *a crapshoot* — American, a situation whose result is pure luck.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To protect yourself against loss or disappointment by supporting more than one option instead of choosing just one.
entries.usage: Common in finance, politics, careers and everyday decisions: *I'm hedging my bets by applying to three schools.* It often takes *by* + -ing, and in politics it can sound cautious or indecisive. The possessive matches the subject: *they hedged their bets*.
examples: I'm **hedging my bets** by applying to three colleges, including one safety school.
Many investors are **hedging their bets** with a mix of stocks and gold.
The coach **hedged his bets**, praising both quarterbacks but refusing to name a starter.

drill.sentence: We weren't sure if it would rain, so we {{hedged our bets}} and reserved both a patio table and one inside.
drill.hint: kept two options open to protect ourselves (not *played it safe*)

entries.related: *keep your options open* — avoid committing to one choice; *cover all your bases* — prepare for every possibility; *put all your eggs in one basket* — the opposite.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: So even that nobody can yet predict or declare who will win.
entries.usage: Mainly a news phrase for elections and sports, especially on election night: *The race is still too close to call.* It usually follows *be* or *remain*. Networks *call* a race when they declare the winner, so the phrase sounds official and cautious.
examples: With ninety percent of the votes counted, the Senate race is still **too close to call**.
The judges said the dance-off was **too close to call** and asked both couples to perform again.
My kids are arguing about who won the race to the car; I told them it was **too close to call**.

drill.sentence: The photo finish was so tight that, for a few minutes, the race was {{too close to call}}.
drill.hint: so even that no winner can be named yet (not *neck and neck*)

entries.related: *neck and neck* — exactly even during a race; *a toss-up* — a situation with an even chance either way; *down to the wire* — until the last moment.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To act in a tough, aggressive and sometimes ruthless way to get what you want, especially in negotiations or politics.
entries.usage: Common in American business, politics and legal news: *The union is ready to play hardball.* It often takes *with* + the opponent, and it can sound admiring or critical depending on the speaker. *Hardball* also works before a noun: *hardball tactics*.
examples: The landlord is **playing hardball**, threatening to evict us if we complain again.
If they won't lower the price, we'll have to **play hardball** and walk away.
Both sides are **playing hardball** in the contract talks, and a strike looks likely.

drill.sentence: The cable company wouldn't lower my bill until I {{played hardball}} and threatened to switch providers.
drill.hint: acted tough and aggressive — a baseball image (not *got tough*)

entries.related: *drive a hard bargain* — negotiate firmly for a good deal; *take the gloves off* — start fighting without restraint; *play nice* — the opposite, be cooperative.
entries.origin: From baseball, called *hardball* to distinguish it from *softball*, which uses a larger, softer ball.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Two things that are so different that comparing them is unfair or meaningless.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and debate to reject a comparison: *That's apples and oranges.* It usually follows *be* or *compare*: *comparing apples and oranges*, *comparing apples to oranges*. British speakers also say *chalk and cheese*, but mostly about two very different people.
examples: A New York salary and a small-town salary are **apples and oranges**; rent alone is three times higher.
You can't judge a high school team against the pros — that's **apples and oranges**.
Comparing today's streaming numbers with old record sales is like comparing **apples and oranges**.

drill.sentence: Sure, my first apartment cost half what yours does, but that was Ohio in 2005; it's {{apples and oranges}}.
drill.hint: two things too different to compare fairly (not *night and day*)

entries.related: *apples to oranges* — same, in *compare apples to oranges*; *chalk and cheese* — British, very different, mostly about people; *night and day* — a huge difference, as in *the difference is night and day*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: The less harmful or less unpleasant of two bad choices.
entries.usage: Common in politics, ethics and everyday decisions: *I voted for the lesser of two evils.* It usually follows *choose*, *pick*, *vote for* or *be*, and the short form *the lesser evil* is also common. It sounds resigned and suggests that neither option is good.
examples: Many voters weren't excited about either candidate and just picked **the lesser of two evils**.
Between a six-hour layover and a red-eye flight, I chose **the lesser of two evils**: the red-eye.
For my knee, surgery seemed like **the lesser of two evils** compared with years of pain.

drill.sentence: Neither pizza place in town is good, but the one by the train station is {{the lesser of two evils}}.
drill.hint: the less bad choice (not *the better option*)

entries.related: *between a rock and a hard place* — facing two equally bad choices; *a necessary evil* — something bad that you have to accept; *the better of two bad options* — plainer.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A weak or distorted version of an opponent's argument, created so that it is easier to attack and defeat.
entries.usage: Common in debates, politics, academic writing and online arguments, almost always as a criticism: *That's a straw man.* It also works before a noun (*a straw man argument*) and, informally, as a verb: *Stop strawmanning me.* In logic it is a recognized fallacy, the *straw man fallacy*.
examples: Nobody said we should ban cars; that's **a straw man**.
My brother turned "maybe we should eat out less" into "you hate my cooking" — a classic **straw man**.
The op-ed attacks **a straw man** version of the proposal, not what the bill actually says.

drill.sentence: She never said kids shouldn't play sports; he set up {{a straw man}} so he could knock it down.
drill.hint: a distorted version of her view that is easy to attack

entries.related: *a red herring* — something that distracts from the real issue; *put words in someone's mouth* — claim someone said what they didn't; *steelman* — the opposite, present the strongest version of an opponent's view.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Clear, decisive evidence that proves who did something wrong or that a claim is true.
entries.usage: Common in news, politics, law and investigations, and often used in the negative: *There's no smoking gun.* It also comes before nouns: *a smoking-gun email*, *smoking-gun evidence*. It suggests proof, not just suspicion.
examples: Investigators found **the smoking gun**: an email from the CEO approving the cover-up.
Doctors suspected the new medication, and the blood test was **the smoking gun**.
Mom never found **a smoking gun**, but the cookie crumbs on my shirt didn't help my case.

drill.sentence: Prosecutors said the security camera video was {{the smoking gun}} that put him at the scene.
drill.hint: the decisive evidence — a weapon image

entries.related: *hard evidence* — solid proof; *circumstantial evidence* — evidence that suggests but does not prove; *a paper trail* — written records that show what happened.
entries.origin: From the image of a gun still smoking just after a shot; it became popular during Watergate, when a 1972 recording that proved Nixon's role in the cover-up was called the *smoking gun* tape.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A controversial topic that provokes strong emotions and divides people, especially in politics.
entries.usage: Mainly a news and politics phrase, common in American journalism for topics that split voters along party lines. It appears as *a hot-button issue* or *topic*, with a hyphen before the noun. Calling something a hot-button issue suggests that discussing it will cause conflict.
examples: Noise from the new runway has become **a hot-button issue** in the suburbs near the airport.
At our house, screen time is **a hot-button issue**; the kids argue about it every night.
Many companies avoid commenting on **hot-button issues** to stay out of politics.

drill.sentence: School start times became {{a hot-button issue}} in our town, with parents shouting at each other during board meetings.
drill.hint: a topic that divides people and stirs strong feelings (not *controversial …*)

entries.related: *a sore subject* — a topic that upsets one person; *a third rail* — a topic politicians avoid because it is dangerous to touch; *divisive* — causing disagreement.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A punishment that is much too mild for the offense, especially one given by an authority.
entries.usage: Common in news and conversation, usually critical of courts, regulators or schools: *The fine was just a slap on the wrist.* It often follows *get*, *receive* or *get off with*, and is often stressed with *just*, *only* or *mere*.
examples: The bank paid a five-million-dollar fine, which is **a slap on the wrist** for a company that size.
My brother crashed Dad's car and got **a slap on the wrist**; I got grounded for a month over a scratch.
Fans were angry that the player got only **a slap on the wrist** for the dangerous hit.

drill.sentence: Despite years of polluting the river, the factory got off with {{a slap on the wrist}}: a small fine and a warning.
drill.hint: a punishment that was far too mild

entries.related: *get off lightly* — receive a milder punishment than expected; *let someone off the hook* — free someone from punishment or duty; *throw the book at someone* — the opposite, punish as severely as possible.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To fail to reach a goal, win a contest, or have the required amount of something.
entries.usage: Common in sports reporting, fundraising and everyday talk: *The team came up short again.* An amount can go before *short* (*came up five hundred dollars short*), and *of* + the target can follow: *came up short of a majority*. It sounds softer and more sympathetic than *lose* or *fail*.
examples: The Bills **came up short** in the playoffs again, losing by a field goal.
The school fundraiser **came up short**, so the new playground will have to wait another year.
I kept **coming up short** on rent, so I took a weekend job.

drill.sentence: She trained hard for the Olympic team but {{came up short}} by a tenth of a second.
drill.hint: failed to make it (not *fell …*)

entries.related: *fall short* — fail to reach a standard, more neutral and common in writing; *miss the cut* — fail to qualify; *come through* — the opposite, succeed when needed.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: Failed or stopped, with no real chance of making progress or succeeding.
entries.usage: Common in politics and business about plans, bills, deals and projects: *The bill is dead in the water.* It usually follows *be*, *look* or *leave*. It is stronger than *stalled*: it suggests the thing is very unlikely to recover.
examples: Once the main investor pulled out, the movie was **dead in the water**.
Without a second income, our plan to open a café is **dead in the water**.
The merger was **dead in the water** once federal regulators objected.

drill.sentence: After the lead singer quit, the band's comeback tour was {{dead in the water}}.
drill.hint: failed, with no chance of moving forward — a boat image

entries.related: *a nonstarter* — an idea with no chance from the start; *stalled* — stopped for now; *dead on arrival* — failed as soon as it was introduced, often about bills.
entries.origin: From sailing: a ship that is dead in the water has stopped moving and has no power or wind.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To keep talking about or pushing an issue that has already been decided or that nobody cares about anymore.
entries.usage: Common in American conversation and meetings, often as an apology or a complaint: *I don't want to beat a dead horse, but …* It sounds a little impatient when said about someone else. British English says *flog a dead horse*, which can also mean wasting effort on a hopeless task.
examples: I know I'm **beating a dead horse**, but please remember to lock the back door.
Can we stop **beating a dead horse**? The vote happened, and the decision is final.
Sports radio hosts keep **beating a dead horse** about that missed call from last season.

drill.sentence: We've discussed the vacation budget five times already; let's not {{beat a dead horse}}.
drill.hint: keep arguing about something already settled (not *flog …*)

entries.related: *flog a dead horse* — the British version; *sound like a broken record* — keep repeating the same thing; *drop it* — stop talking about it.

entries.term: the devil is in the details
entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: A plan or idea may look simple in general, but the small details are where the real problems are hidden.
entries.usage: Common in politics, business and negotiations, usually as a warning about agreements and plans that sound good. It is often contracted to *the devil's in the details*. It suggests caution, not rejection.
examples: Both sides agree on a new contract in principle, but **the devil is in the details**.
Building your own house sounds romantic; **the devil's in the details**, like permits and plumbing.
The gym membership looked cheap, but **the devil was in the details**: a two-hundred-dollar cancellation fee.

drill.sentence: Planning a cheap European vacation sounds easy, but {{the devil is in the details}}: train strikes, hidden fees and closed museums.
drill.hint: the small print hides the real problems (a saying)

entries.related: *read the fine print* — check the small details of a contract; *easier said than done* — simple to suggest but hard to do; *God is in the details* — an older saying: details deserve care.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: To end up back in the same position or situation where you started, after a series of changes.
entries.usage: Common in stories, journalism and reflection on careers, fashion and life: *Things have come full circle.* It can sound satisfying or ironic, depending on the story. Typical subjects are *life*, *fashion*, *things* or a person: *I've come full circle.*
examples: Dad started out at the local newspaper, and forty years later he's back there as editor; he's **come full circle**.
Fashion has **come full circle**, and my teenage daughter now wears the jeans I wore in the nineties.
After decades of big-box stores, our town has **come full circle**, with small shops returning to Main Street.

drill.sentence: I left Boston after college, lived abroad for twenty years, and now I'm teaching at my old high school. I've {{come full circle}}.
drill.hint: ended up back where I started — a geometry image

entries.related: *back to square one* — back at the start because something failed; *history repeats itself* — the same kind of events happen again.
entries.origin: From Shakespeare's *King Lear*: *The wheel is come full circle*.

entries.label: idiom
entries.meaning: It is easy to see the right decision once you know what happened, but it was not obvious at the time.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and analysis, usually to excuse a past decision or to stop unfair criticism of it: *Well, hindsight is 20/20.* It comes from *20/20 vision* (said *twenty-twenty*), the American term for normal, sharp eyesight. A British equivalent is *it's easy to be wise after the event*.
examples: Everyone says we should have refinanced when rates were low, but **hindsight is twenty-twenty**.
Fans blame the coach for the late substitution, but **hindsight is twenty-twenty**.
I know, I should have seen the warning signs in that relationship. **Hindsight is twenty-twenty**.

drill.sentence: Don't beat yourself up about taking that job; you couldn't have known the company would close. {{Hindsight is twenty-twenty}}.
drill.hint: it's easy to judge once you know the outcome — an eyesight saying

entries.related: *Monday-morning quarterbacking* — American, criticizing decisions after you know the result; *wise after the event* — British, knowing the right answer too late.
